title: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of h
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of hundreds of prisoners.Burnham announced last week that he was pausing the scheme, which would have seen about 700 prisoners freed in the first phase in September, following a backlash from survivors and victims.But the Conservatives say the government's review will not stop offenders being released. The scheme was part of a bid to stop unprecedented overcrowding, which Labour says was caused by Conservative governments failing to build new prisons.A Labour spokesperson said: "It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess."On Tuesday, Burnham said: "It is a challenging situation and we shouldn't actually be in this position as a country, but we have to deal with the reality of where we are."But I will do anything I can to minimise risk to the public and that is why I am looking again and why I have put the release plan for September on hold and we'll make further statements on this in due course."Early release was used by the Conservative government, external in 2023 because of prison overcrowding, first for 18 and then 70 days, and 10,000 prisoners had been released early by June 2024 - before Labour came to power.When Sir Keir Starmer entered Downing Street in July 2024, there were fewer than 100 spare prison places across the adult male estate, which is what prompted the Sentencing Act to release another 6,000 prisoners early from September.While the act already excludes some of the most serious and dangerous offenders, such as murderers serving life sentences or those on extended sentences, the eligibility for early release is based on the length of fixed sentence, external, rather than the type of offence.That means some criminals convicted of serious sexual and violent offences who have a fixed release date will leave prison earlier than they had expected - although subject to monitoring and risk of recall to prison.Badenoch is calling on Burnham to fast-track legislation to keep serious offenders behind bars.Speaking at a press conference alongside victims who could be impacted by the changes, the Conservative leader said: "It's quite clear that the prime minister sees that this is a problem, but I don't think he knows what to do about it."She said she was concerned the pause would be "yet another thing where there will be warm words and nothing happens". Without emergency legislation, Badenoch says dangerous offenders will start to be released the day after MPs return to Parliament after the summer recess on Tuesday 1 September.She is calling on Burnham to revoke legislation coming into effect on 2 September and if necessary recall Parliament to ensure the worst violent and sexual offenders are exempted from early release.Asked if the problem of prison overcrowding was a failing of the last Conservative government, she said the "crisis" had been "long time coming". "We did something, it wasn't enough, I'm sorry about that," she said, adding: "I can't fix the past, what I can do is come up with solutions."She said that to solve the problem of prison overcrowding in the long-run, the public needed to accept that some prisons would have to be built in their communities. She also urged the government to consider renting prison places overseas.Successive UK governments have explored the idea of sending prisoners to Estonia, however in 2025 the BBC was told that Conservative and Labour ministers had decided the plans would be too expensive. Earlier this month, the Conservative front bench sought to put pressure on the government to rethink the earlier release plans, saying that it would mean some rapists would leave prison sooner than expected. The government stood by the plan, saying it was a political choice to manage offenders on strict conditions in the community, rather than see the collapse of the system, leaving sex offenders and others to act with impunity.Burnham's decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added.PC Harper's widow Lissie called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.Defending the review of the Sentencing Act that has been announced by Burnham, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives have some nerve. "During their 14 years in office, they shut 23 prisons, created just 482 jail places, and granted early release to 10,000 prisoners - leaving the criminal justice system teetering on verge of collapse."It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess. We have already delivered over 3,000 prison places and we're investing billions to deliver thousands more."Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller MP said: "The reality is that in a properly functioning justice system, no victim or loved ones should ever be told that their perpetrator is being released earlier than expected."Unfortunately, the Conservatives left our prisons on the brink of collapse, creating a capacity crisis that required emergency action to keep the system functioning and the public safe."Now that the government claims to have increased prison capacity, there is a clear opportunity for Burnham to correct some of the mistakes made by his predecessors with this scheme."Reform UK's Home Affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the "disastrous" policy had been introduced by the Tories, and Badenoch had in 2024 supported efforts to expand it."It's clear that only one party has consistently opposed early release and proposed strong law and order reforms to ensure hardened criminals are locked up for the full duration of their sentences," Yusuf said in a statement."Only Reform UK will fix lawless Britain," the party's Home Affairs spokesperson added.Clarification Tuesday 28 July: A previous version of this story said the act already excludes the most serious and dangerous offenders and the eligibility for early release is based on the length of sentence. We have clarified to say that some of the most serious offenders are excluded and the eligibility is based on the length of a fixed sentence.

schema.headline: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme

title: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez
description: Figure caption, BBC reports from outside court after judge rules singer D4vd will stand trial for murderBySareen HabeshianShaimaa Khalil and Sam Mulic
body: Figure caption, BBC reports from outside court after judge rules singer D4vd will stand trial for murderBySareen HabeshianShaimaa Khalil and Sam MulickReporting fromcourthouse in Los AngelesUpdated 8 hours agoA judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of a teenage girl.The decision came after a five-day preliminary hearing, in which Los Angeles prosecutors questioned a dozen witnesses and displayed graphic photographic evidence as 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez's family watched on.The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, is accused of killing the girl, whose remains were found last September in a Tesla registered to his address.Burke, 21, has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing her.Burke is scheduled to be charged on 31 August. The trial is to start within 90 days of that date.Prosecutors have alleged Burke stabbed the teen before dismembering her body after years of sexual abuse.They allege he killed her because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.Evidence read in court on Monday showed threats Hernandez made to Burke on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl."I swear to GOD I will kill u", one expletive-laden text said, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on.The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.During questioning at the hearing on Monday, Detective Corey Farrell of the Los Angeles Police Department said text messages indicated that the defendant and the girl had attended church with her family.  In response to the defence, the detective said he was aware the teen had misrepresented her age to the defendant, telling him she was 16 and 18 at different times.Burke's defence lawyers argued there was not sufficient evidence that he had committed the crime.They said her parents were aware of what was going on between them and had even given written consent for her to travel to London with Burke for a week. The defence highlighted texts on the 22nd and the 23rd of April that suggested Celeste had insisted on going to Burke's Hollywood Hills home and that he had argued against her coming before agreeing to send her an Uber on the night of the 23rd.He "repeatedly expressed love and care for Ms Hernandez after they broke up", defence attorney Marilyn Bednarski said in court.The medical examiner's inability to prove how the two penetrating wounds found in the girl occurred and the lack of surveillance video capturing Burke being home on the night of 23 April showed a lack of evidence, the defence argued.Image source, Getty ImagesLos Angeles County Superior Court Judge Charlaine Olmedo ruled that evidence presented during the preliminary hearing provided probable cause for a trial.Burke is charged with murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14, and unlawful mutilation of human remains."The people have met their burden on all counts," Judge Olmedo said.She found that prosecutors met the threshold for the charge of murder with special circumstances, including lying in wait, motive for financial gain and eliminating a witness.Following the hearing, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said his office only presented a fraction of the evidence it had against Burke, and that it would present everything in the coming trial.Hochman also said his office had not yet determined if it would pursue the death penalty against Burke.Listen to the BBC's Fame Under Fire podcast which brings you the latest from inside the Los Angeles courtroom at the D4vd preliminary hearing.Gruesome images of the girl's dismembered corpse were shown in court during the preliminary hearing.A homicide detective testified that Burke had ordered a body bag, chainsaws, an inflatable pool and a shovel online in the days after Celeste's death.Prosecutors highlighted records that revealed Burke ordered chainsaws and a shovel to his residence after April 23. They allege he used a chainsaw to dismember Hernadez's body.However, Los Angeles Police Department criminalist Lauren Wallace testified that the chainsaws found in his garage tested negative for the presence of blood and were not tested for DNA thereafter, a point the defence highlighted in their attempt to prove the evidence presented was inconclusive.However, investigators were unable to locate a third, 10-inch Makita chainsaw, which prosecutors claim Burke also ordered following Hernandez's death.

schema.headline: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez

title: Reform UK reporting Green leader Zack Polanski to police over Instagram post
description: Reform UK have reported Green Party leader Zack Polanski to the police, after he shared an Instagram post including a photo of a man wearing a top fea
body: Reform UK have reported Green Party leader Zack Polanski to the police, after he shared an Instagram post including a photo of a man wearing a top featuring the name "Nigel" alongside an image of a guillotine.One of several images showed a man in a black t-shirt with a large guillotine below the words "We're only making plans for Nigel".Sharing a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."A Green Party spokesperson said: "Once this image was brought to [Zack's] attention he immediately unshared the post. He unequivocally does not support this type of dangerous message."Polanski had shared the photo with his 713,000 followers in a post containing several pictures of a Green Party event on Sunday, having accepted a request to collaborate with another account.In a post on X, the Metropolitan Police said: "We received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media. We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting enquiries into the matter."The words "We're only making plans for Nigel" are the same as the lyrics of a 1979 song by band XTC, external.The Green Party spokesperson said: "Zack condemns the image on the T-shirt. He was tagged in a post with 20 images and clicked accept without realising there was more to it than he had seen."The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself."He and the Green Party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division."The BBC understands Polanski has not been contacted by police.Reform UK say Polanski has not been in touch with Farage to privately apologise for sharing the post. The Greens have been approached for comment in relation to this.A photographer with the username just.barold claimed responsibility, external for the photo, which he said was of someone wearing a satirical T-shirt, and apologised to Polanski on X, saying "this is not his fault" and adding he had reported himself to the police.In a series of posts, the freelance photographer said: "This wasn't intended to offend anyone and it's clearly not intended as a serious threat to anyone's safety whatsoever."They added: "This performative outrage is just that, and if people want to come and take it out on someone then take it out on the person who took the picture, and who then posted it."However, Reform's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the image showed "a photo of man calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage", which he claimed could be an "incitement to murder".Yusuf confirmed Reform UK had reported the post to police and will also report Polanski to to the monitoring officer at the Greater London Assembly, where the Green leader is an elected member."To do this just two weeks after our friend Ann was murdered is staggering," Yusuf said. "This is incitement to murder. It should be treated as such by the police."Incitement to violence is recognised as an offence under UK law.Prosecutions can be brought under the Public Order Act 1986, which covers "threatening, abusive or insulting" behaviour with intent to cause or provoke "the immediate use of unlawful violence" against a person.Prominent Reform member Widdecombe, 78, was found dead in her home in Haytor, Devon, on 9 July. Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder. Her death reignited a row about the security of political figures in public life, with this year marking the 10th anniversary of the murder of Labour MP Jo Cox and the fifth anniversary of the murder of Conservative MP David Amess.Following Widdecombe's death, Polanski called for all party leaders to get extra security.Asked about Widdecombe's death at the time, he told BBC Breakfast: "I am worried and I have been worried for a long time."I would encourage the government to provide me with extra security, but that is a choice for them."Andy Burnham also backed a serious review of MPs' security earlier this month.Reform UK's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick had accused the government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's security, after it emerged the party turned down a government-funded security offer last year.The Home Office said Jenrick's comments were "categorically untrue", and that independent security experts, not ministers, held responsibility for deciding MPs' security.

schema.headline: Reform UK reporting Green leader Zack Polanski to police over Instagram post

title: Ariana Grande sues hackers who leaked music and videos
description: Pop star Ariana Grande has filed a lawsuit against two unidentified hackers who, she claims, leaked unreleased music and studio footage after gaining
body: Pop star Ariana Grande has filed a lawsuit against two unidentified hackers who, she claims, leaked unreleased music and studio footage after gaining access to her collaborators' computers.In papers filed in Los Angeles and reported by US media outlets, the singer alleged the hackers had targeted photographers and producers' in order to access material that was sold "on the dark web" for "significant sums of money"."In 2023 alone, 45 unreleased songs belonging to Ms Grande were hacked, stolen, and leaked," the documents said. "Since her music debut in 2011, hundreds of similar leaks have taken place."Her lawyers said she was initiating legal action to uncover the identity of the hackers.Grande has previously expressed her desire to hold hackers accountable for leaking unreleased music.During an interview with the Zach Sang show in 2024, she spoke about a song called Fantasize, written with Swedish pop savant Max Martin, which went viral after being posted online."Before I left for Wicked - [there were] a few studio sessions that I did which are all over TikTok, thank you so much, I'll see you in jail. Literally," she said."Those were all written for a TV show, for something that was not for me, so Fantasize comes out, crazy, was stolen... These pirates, crooks, illegal!"Her legal case outlined an alleged pattern of illegal behaviour, in which the accounts of Grande's co-workers were systematically targeted over several years.In 2025, it claimed, the defendants hacked into the mobile device of a producer who had collaborated with Grande and accessed unreleased masters, demos and footage from recording sessions.The previous year, the suit claimed, hackers created an email account impersonating a photographer, and persuaded a digital technician to send them unreleased photos that belonged to Grande.The singer accused the hackers of violating the "sacred relationship that exists between her and her fans" and is suing for invasion of privacy, violation of California computer hacking laws, and conversion. Her lawyers said the "malicious invasion of Ms. Grande's privacy and disruption of her career have caused her substantial and irreparable harm due to this breach of privacy."The court filing comes as Grande prepares for the release of her eighth studio album, Petal, this Friday.She is currently in the middle of a world tour, which is due to hit the UK in August.Grande previously hinted the concerts would be her last for "a long time"."I'm going to give it my all and it's going to be beautiful," she told Amy Poehler's Good Hang podcast, external. "I think that's why I'm doing it because I'm like: 'One last hurrah' - for now."

schema.headline: Ariana Grande sues hackers who leaked music and videos

title: Naga Munchetty swaps BBC One's Breakfast for Radio 5 Live Breakfast
description: Munchetty is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about £360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.She has i
body: Munchetty is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about £360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct. That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.The BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously.Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

schema.headline: Naga Munchetty swaps BBC One's Breakfast for Radio 5 Live Breakfast

title: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks
description: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on hu
body: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on human rights to that of authoritarian states.The diplomatic row was initially sparked last week, when the US joined North Korea and Russia in voting against extending Volker Turk's term as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. After the vote on Friday, France's UN mission criticised the US and compared it to North Korea and Russia. "The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore," it posted on X, external.In response, US ambassador Mike Waltz accused France of voting for a human rights chief who had been "lecturing" democratic countries while "cozying up to the world's worst oppressors", without elaborating on what he meant.Turk has criticised Russia's war in Ukraine and Israel's military conduct in Gaza.The US team's walkout came while France's ambassador Jerome Bonnafont was speaking during an emergency Security Council meeting on Russia's war in Ukraine.US ambassador Dan Negrea said the delegation would continue to make similar protests until France "renounces their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric".The fight over Turk's second term, which was passed with 144 states in favour, 10 against and 13 abstentions, reflects tensions between Washington and the United Nations.The Trump administration has cut funding for UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of its entities.On Friday, US ambassador Jeff Bartos criticised Turk's reappointment and said "there will be consequences" to the assembly which "tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts". "The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding," he said.However, French ambassador Bonnafont described Turk as "a voice of conscience" who demonstrated "rigor and impartiality" during his first term.Deputy UN spokesperson Farhan Haq declined to comment on the US walkout, adding the UN expected all member states to respect the decision.

schema.headline: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks

title: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'
description: "The release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate," Wilson noted. "This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas... translations of Odyssey
body: "The release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate," Wilson noted. "This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas... translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves... [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments."Nolan... is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful."But she was left largely disappointed by the three-hour epic"I had hoped that Nolan's affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters," she wrote."But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality... the film's vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants."Wilson added that her teenagers had "had a good time" seeing the blockbuster at the cinema."It's a family-friendly audiovisual spectacle, like an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display - and with about the same level of narrative and emotional depth," she said."There are more female characters than in most Nolan movies, thanks to the source material. But none of them has much to say, in contrast to the characterisations in the poem."During his press tour for the film, Sir Christopher told Empire magazine, external that he used the opening line of Wilson's translation ("Tell me about a complicated man") as a guide for his Odysseus, played by Matt Damon.In contrast to Wilson's take, the latest adaptation has received rapturous reviews from film critics.It is the director's first movie since 2023's Oppenheimer, which won the Academy Award for best picture.The Telegraph declared The Odyssey the "film of the year", while Metro added that the movie would "change cinema forever".The Times described it as "a masterpiece in every way", and the Standard praised the film as a "colossal piece of cinema".The Odyssey, which was released earlier this month, stars Matt Damon, Zendaya, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, Anne Hathaway, Charlize Theron and Lupita Nyong'o.It follows Odysseus (Damon), the Greek king of Ithaca, on his long and perilous journey home from the Trojan War to rescue his wife and son (Hathaway and Holland).

schema.headline: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'

title: West Indies v Pakistan: Justin Greaves takes five wickets for none in incredible spell
description: First Test, Tarouba (day three of five)West Indies 311 (Hope 92; Ali 4-50) & 126-7 (Chanderpaul 35, Abbas 3-14)Pakistan 282 (Masood 109; Greaves 5-27)
body: First Test, Tarouba (day three of five)West Indies 311 (Hope 92; Ali 4-50) & 126-7 (Chanderpaul 35, Abbas 3-14)Pakistan 282 (Masood 109; Greaves 5-27)West Indies lead by 155 runsScorecardWest Indies all-rounder Justin Greaves took five wickets without conceding a run in an incredible spell of bowling on day three of the first Test against Pakistan.Greaves, who is playing in his 17th Test, claimed his maiden Test five-wicket haul to help dismiss Pakistan for 282 in response to West Indies' first-innings total of 311.The 32-year-old Barbadian's spell - five consecutive wicket maidens - was all the more remarkable given he had bowled six overs earlier in the day for 27 runs without taking a wicket."When I came on captain Roston Chase just said 'continue to be disciplined in what you are doing' and to see if I can get some wickets for the team," Greaves said."The ball nipped around and I got some reward. Anytime I get the ball in hand the team looks to me to be that solid player for them [and] try to dig us out of situations."To get five wickets for the first time in Test cricket, I'm really happy, but there's still a lot of work to do in the game."Former Pakistan captain Shan Masood was Greaves' first wicket at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy in Trinidad when he was bowled for 109 in the 64th over following a superb set-up.Greaves had pushed the ball wide to the left-hander from over the wicket before he tailed a delivery back into Masood who played down the wrong line and inside edged on to his stumps.Aamer Jamal had his middle stump uprooted in Greaves' next over as the seamer speared one through his defences.Greaves then trapped Ali Usman lbw before he had Mohammed Rizwan and Mohammad Abbas both caught behind as Pakistan lost their last seven wickets for just 38 runs.West Indies reached stumps on day three on 126-7 in their second innings - a lead of 155 runs - to leave the match finely poised.

schema.headline: West Indies v Pakistan: Justin Greaves takes five wickets for none in incredible spell

title: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress
description: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with t
body: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with the sun disappearing behind", with an "orange-like filter" over the city.Though De Abreu said he is less concerned about his flat which lies on the other side of the river, he "can see a number of people worried about what is to come".Elsewhere, Rachel Hanberry told BBC Radio 5 Live that her beachfront home in Biscarrosse Plage, which lies about 63km (40 miles) from Bordeaux, is located next to the town's evacuation point. "Everyone came here on Thursday night," she said. "People had nowhere to go. We offered our home to people."The community there has "lost so much", she added. "The stress and trauma that you feel as someone living here is immense." About 700km away, in Cotignac in the south-east of France, Jo Barnes and her family returned to their home on Saturday, having evacuated for four days after a fire rapidly moved towards their property. "A wall of orange flames came roaring up over the hill," Barnes said. "On Friday afternoon, the fire came back to our area... within 10 metres of the back of our house, we have a gas tank here, it was all very dramatic." Though the surrounding hillside was blackened and charred, the town of Cotignac was undamaged and the Barnes' family home left intact. In the central Madrid region of Spain, where more than 27,000 hectares (66,000 acres) have burnt, residents have faced similar ordeals. "Everyone had to get out of the village quickly, it was a critical situation and people were scared," Olga Congacha told AFP news agency.She and her husband did not take much: "[We] left with all that we could grab, our important documents, some clothes".In the eastern Castellón province, Ricardo Pozo told AFP that he had "never seen a fire this intense before". "I've seen major fires, but on television. Nothing like this, here and now." Maria Garcia, who lives in Betxí - also in the Castellón province - described to Reuters how the fires had put life on pause for those who evacuated: "You can't go out to work, you can't go about your daily life." "You can see the mountains you've known your whole life burning," she added.The wildfires have also upended plans for holidaymakers. James Hillier had been visiting his son in the seaside community of Lacanau about 42 km (26 miles) east of Bordeaux in the Gironde department."The whole town got consumed by smoke," he told the BBC. "There was ash falling from the sky and I noticed a big lump of it landed on my hand."He and his wife left the town for Bordeaux on Saturday, but found that in the city "the air was acrid - it stung your eyes and people were wearing masks". They have since left to go to somewhere in the north of the France instead. Sarah from Hertfordshire realised that her family would have to cut their week-long holiday in Bordeaux short because of the smoke. "We sealed all the apartment up, but it still had a really strong smell of smoke everywhere. It was quite worrying," she said.She then warned her sister-in-law Georgia, whose family had been due to join them in the Bordeaux region in Lacanau, not to come. Georgia booked to stay in another region instead.Georgia said she has not been able to secure a refund from her accommodation operator because the fire had not yet reached Lacanau at the time of cancellation. "If we don't find a solution with them we currently stand to lose over £3,500," Georgia added.

schema.headline: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress

title: Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14, Burnham says
description: Secondary school pupils in England will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning under reforms outlin
body: Secondary school pupils in England will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning under reforms outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.The government said the courses, which would be available from Year 10, would be linked to local industries and designed to give children a clearer pathway into work.Data published this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, the highest level in more than 12 years.Few details have been published about how the new vocational courses would work in practice and it is not clear how they would operate in areas with low industrial activity.The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.Speaking at a train manufacturing site in Derby, Burnham said: "We've had a system built for too long around the university route and it sends a message to some young people that they're some kind of second-class citizens, and it's just not right."They need an education system that works for them as well, that offers a path to all young people, that's balanced between academic and technical."The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet" - but declined to put a target date on his ambition."The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said."It's hard to put a firm date on the moment when you can say there are fewer than now."However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said while there was a "broad consensus" on improving vocational education, it was "not a big bold announcement".She told BBC Breakfast: "What's going on there is a drastic shortage of jobs because Labour's policies over the last couple of years have killed job opportunities for young people. This announcement will not solve that."Under the proposals, pupils would continue to study core maths, English and science but would also have the option of combining the subjects with technical education.It will include the chance to gain work experience and create connections with local employers, Burnham said, with the government saying the policy will eventually drive down the amount spent on welfare for young people.While some business leaders welcomed the move, others said youth jobs could be boosted by other means.Jon White, chief financial officer at building materials firm Huws Gray, said employers were "struggling" with a lack of incentives to hire younger people, pointing to the government narrowing the gap between the national minimum wage for under-21s and the national living wage.He also said the government should change the rules around how employers can spend the apprenticeship levy. The levy is paid by big employers, with the money raised available to all businesses to help fund apprenticeship training - but White said businesses should be allowed to use it to pay young people's wages as well.For schools, the Association of School and College Leaders said they welcomed the prime minister's ambition, but warned that schools could face capacity issues as they continued to face tight budgets and implemented radical reforms to special education needs.The National Education Union said the new proposals would "hit the skids unless there is sufficient investment in schools", while the NAHT school leaders' union called for "greater clarity" about funding and practical details.Along with the changes to learning, Ofsted will change the way it measures performance and will inspect for technical education, but it is not clear how this will fit alongside national measures designed to hold schools to account.Tuesday's announcement is the latest in a series of policies in recent years designed to offer a vocational route in education as a counter-balance to high numbers of young people going to university. In 2020, T-levels were introduced as a technical education alternative to A-Levels in England, with courses including construction, agriculture and health.Former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced earlier this year that V-levels would be an additional vocational option for students post-16 from 2027.Where T-levels are a set course broadly equivalent to three A-levels, V-levels would be equivalent to one A-level, allowing students to mix and match academic and vocational subjects.The changes announced on Tuesday will only impact England, but improving access to technical and vocational education has been a common focus for governments in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland too in recent years.The policy will build on local initiatives like the MBacc, or Greater Manchester Baccalaureate, which was launched in September 2024 by Burnham when he was the city's mayor.It has provided a framework for pupils to pick GCSE subjects in both academic and technical subjects which align with growing local industries, like green energy or digital.Teenagers under this programme have also been promised more careers advice and work experience that links to seven sectors of work.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the announcement marked the "start of a real shared effort with employers, businesses, mayors and councils to design an education system that connects young people to jobs and careers in their local area".In May, an interim report by former Alan Milburn warned the number of young people not in employment, education or training risked leading to a "lost generation".That report was published the same day as figures from the Office for National Statistics showed more than one in eight of UK 16- to 24-year-olds were Neet at the start of this year.Milburn said the changes announced by Burnham were "consistent with the findings of my review".Liberal Democrat education spokesperson Munira Wilson said there had to be provisions to allow pupils flexibility to "change direction and move between 'academic' and 'technical'"."We must not allow these changes to predetermine children's futures at just 14, baking in disadvantage," she added.

schema.headline: Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14, Burnham says

title: Zinedine Zidane: Former Real Madrid manager appointed as France head coach
description: Former Real Madrid manager Zinedine Zidane has been confirmed as the head coach of the France national team.Didier Deschamps, France's longest-serving
body: Former Real Madrid manager Zinedine Zidane has been confirmed as the head coach of the France national team.Didier Deschamps, France's longest-serving manager, ended his 14-year stint in charge after the nation's semi-final exit to Spain at the 2026 World Cup. Zidane, a World Cup winner with France in 1998, has been out of management since leaving Real Madrid for a second time as head coach in 2021. The 54-year-old, widely considered to be France's greatest player, will sign a contract that will see him lead the nation through the 2030 World Cup qualifiers. On being appointed, he said it was "a great source of pride" to lead the French national side following their fourth-place finish at the World Cup."I've often said it: there's nothing greater than the French national team. So it's a joy and obviously a great source of pride to become the manager of this French national team," he added."It's also a responsibility. I want to thank [French Football Federation] president Philippe Diallo, the executive committee, and the French Football Federation for their confidence and acknowledge the 14 years of service from Didier and his staff. "I also have a special thought today for all my coaches. Needless to say, I have high ambitions for the French national team."Diallo described the new head coach as a "legend" of French football."The appointment of Zinedine Zidane as head coach of the French national team is a source of immense pride for the French Football Federation," he said."It marks the meeting of a legend in the history of Les Bleus, who has become one of the most decorated and respected coaches of his generation, and a team with rare potential, driven by the highest ambitions."Zidane's predecessor Deschamps guided France to three major finals over his 14-year reign, helping the country to their second World Cup success with victory in 2018.Zidane's first competitive fixture in charge will be a Nations League trip to Turkey on 25 September.After retiring as a player following the 2006 World Cup, Zidane did not enter management until 2014, when he became coach of Real Madrid Castilla - the club's B team.He stepped up to become the first team manager in January 2016, and by the end of that season had led them to Champions League success with a victory over city rivals Atletico Madrid in the final on penalties.That was the first of three successive Champions League titles for Madrid, making them the first club to win back-to-back European crowns in the Champions League era, and the first to win three titles in a row since Bayern Munich in 1976.He also won La Liga in 2016-17, but departed after the following season, saying change was needed at the Bernabeu.However, Zidane returned to Madrid in March 2019 with the club in poor form, and won another Spanish league title in 2019-20.He also oversaw a period of extensive spending at Madrid, including the signings of Eden Hazard and Rodrygo.But Zidane left at the end of a trophyless 2020-21 campaign, and has not managed since.Zidane has long been courted to become France manager and was first linked with the job after the team was knocked out of the 2010 World Cup in the group stage.Some 16 years later, he has finally taken on the role and will lead the French into qualifying for Euro 2028.Zidane started his playing career at Cannes in 1989, then played for Bordeaux until joining Juventus in 1996.An attacking midfielder, he helped the Italian side win back-to-back Serie A titles and reach successive Champions League finals, before joining Real Madrid in 2001.Zidane moved for £66 million, then the world record transfer fee, as part of Real Madrid's Galacticos era alongside other global stars including Ronaldo, Luis Figo and David Beckham.He began delivering on that fee in the 2002 Champions League final, scoring a stunning volleyed winner as Madrid beat Bayer Leverkusen 2-1 at Hampden Park.For the France national team, Zidane made his greatest contribution as a player with two headed goals in the 1998 World Cup final in Paris.France beat Brazil 3-0 to win the World Cup for the first time, and Zidane won the Ballon d'Or later that year.Zidane was also part of the France team that won Euro 2000, but endured disappointing campaigns in the 2002 World Cup and Euro 2004.He retired from international football in 2004, but was persuaded to return during qualifying for the 2006 World Cup.Zidane was a key player in France advancing through the knock-out stages to the final against Italy - his final match as a professional footballer - and scored the opener with a Panenka penalty off the crossbar after seven minutes.But Italy equalised and the game went to extra time, during which Zidane headbutted Marco Materazzi and was dismissed. Italy went on to win the final on penalties.

schema.headline: Zinedine Zidane: Former Real Madrid manager appointed as France head coach

title: How afraid should we be of Scotland's jellyfish?
description: Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, July and August are peak months for jellyfish sightings in ScotlandByClaire ThomsonBBC ScotlandWh
body: Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, July and August are peak months for jellyfish sightings in ScotlandByClaire ThomsonBBC ScotlandWhen scuba diver and underwater photographer Ross McLaren encountered a jellyfish for the first time, he said all he felt was "sheer terror". "I was diving in the Clyde and one of the instructors had to pull me out of the way of the tentacles as it was wafting above me," he said. McLaren ended up with a sting across his upper lip but said it did not stop him from wanting to dive.Many people are scared of jellyfish due to the fear of painful stings and the creature's unpredictable nature in the water.Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Scuba diver Ross McLaren has completed almost 600 dives since 2016But McLaren, who lives near the coast in North Ayrshire, believes there is more to the brainless, heartless and boneless invertebrates than people might think. "Jellyfish have such a bad reputation but they are one of the most mesmerising and beautiful creatures underwater," he said, having completed almost 600 dives.As we reach peak jellyfish season in Scotland, should we see them as a sight to behold or a reason to run?When do you see the most jellyfish in Scotland?July and August are peak months for jellyfish sightings in Scotland."The number and distribution of jellyfish are impacted by many different factors," said Anna Bunney of the Marine Conservation Society, which runs a nationwide survey of jellyfish."This includes sea temperatures, the availability of plankton for feeding, which peaks during the summer months when it is warmer, and ocean currents."Sea temperatures tend to lag behind air temperatures, Bunney says.The maximum air temperatures in Scotland usually occur in July and August, whereas sea temperatures are at the warmest in August and September.When the sea starts to get warmer, it means a return of the jellyfish.Image source, James LynottImage caption, Sea temperatures, the availability of plankton, and ocean currents have an impact on jellyfish sightings in ScotlandBunney described jellyfish as weak swimmers or "passive drifters" which rely on ocean currents to carry them. Calmer ocean conditions around the UK in the summer months help to push jellyfish gently towards the shore, meaning there are often more sightings of the creatures.Breeding speed also increases with warmer conditions, allowing adult jellyfish to reproduce in large numbers, creating so-called blooms.These blooms can look like a thick soup or pulsing cloud in the water and have been known to block boat engines. In 2011, Torness nuclear power station in East Lothian was even shut down as a precautionary measure due to huge numbers of jellyfish found in sea water entering the plant.Image source, Marc KilpatrickImage caption, A bloom of moon jellyfish washed up on Seafield Beach in Kirkcaldy, Fife, in JulyMcLaren added that while jellyfish season is normally April to October, the creatures can still be seen in Scotland's waters all year round."You see them in the winter months but they are far more prevalent and common during the summer," he said.What happens if a jellyfish stings you?Jellyfish stings in Scotland are not usually life-threatening but can be very painful.Depending on the type of jellyfish, the stingers may not be sharp enough or long enough to pierce the skin.Bunney said most jellyfish have stinging cells but the severity and detectability of the sting varies widely between species.Swimmers should be aware of the Lion's Mane, which is a brownish orange colour, and prevalent around Scotland's coastline in the warmer summer months. They have long tentacles which can give a sore but not lethal sting.The tentacles can break off and float around in the sea or become attached to chains on a boat, for example, but the stinging cells will stay alive even when not attached to the main body.Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, The Lion's Mane jellyfish have long tentacles which can give painful stingsBunney, who said she has been stung a lot by jellyfish, compared a mild sting to that of a nettle."There was one point when every time over a period of two years I was stung by a jellyfish when I was out in the sea," she said."But thankfully, it hasn't impacted how I feel about the ocean."In fact, what I often think is the most frustrating is when you are stung but you cannot see what you have been stung by."Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, The Barrel jellyfish has eight arms and is not normally harmful to humansMcLaren said he has never been put off scuba diving by the prospect of a jellyfish sting but he can understand why swimmers might be nervous."When you're diving, as long as the visibility is good, you can negotiate your way around a jellyfish relatively easily, if you know what way the current is flowing and you pay attention," he said. "Swimming, on the other hand, I totally get it - if I was taking my kids down to the beach and there were a lot of jellyfish I would probably stop them from getting in the water."When you're swimming you tend to have your head out of the water more so you can't always see what is underneath or know where the tentacles are going."Both Bunney and McLaren added that it is important not to touch a jellyfish when it is washed up on a beach as it can still sting, even when presumed dead.Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Jellyfish tentacles can still sting when not attached to the main bodyBunney said to follow NHS guidance after a jellyfish sting.It suggests using tweezers or the edge of a bank card to remove the tentacles as soon as possible as they can continue to sting while attached to the body.A heat pack or immersion in hot water can reduce pain and swelling, and painkillers such as paracetamol can also help. If symptoms because more severe or a sensitive part of body has been stung, seek medical help. Why do jellyfish sting?Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Jellyfish sting as an automatic reflex, not a deliberate attackUnlike bees or wasps, which sting as a defence mechanism to protect themselves, a jellyfish sting is an automatic reflex, not a deliberate attack."A common misconception is jellyfish go after people but contact with a jellyfish is actually merely incidental and humans are not on their menu," Bunney said."They are not actively stinging, it is just when anything touches their tentacles as they are moving through the water, regardless of what it is."Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Small fish often live among jellyfish tentacles for protectionJellyfish tentacles are lined with thousands of venom-filled stinging cells. When touched, these cells fire toxic harpoon-like tubes designed to paralyse prey, such as plankton and small fish.Should jellyfish stop you from swimming in the sea?"Do not be afraid but be cautious" is the advice from Bunney, who generally recommends swimming calmly away from jellyfish."Most of the species found in Scotland have very mild stings, which only cause minor irritation, and some are completely harmless," she said.Bunney says it is important for people to learn about the different species of jellyfish and report sightings to the Marine Conservation Society."People think jellyfish are ugly," she said. "But they are really beautiful creatures that come in all different colours and sizes."Image source, R.S. McLaren PhotographyImage caption, Bunney said most species found in Scotland only have mild stingsMcLaren echoed the love for the marine invertebrate. "People hate jellyfish but I always do my best to take a photo of one when I see it because they are impressive to see in the water," he said."It's almost like stars in the night sky when you are on the sea floor and looking up at the jellyfish above you."It's magical."

schema.headline: How afraid should we be of Scotland's jellyfish?

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty wins bronze again - can he get back to top?
description: Is struggling Ramsay-Peaty nearing the end?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Adam Ramsay-Peaty has not won a major gold medal since the 2022 Co
body: Is struggling Ramsay-Peaty nearing the end?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Adam Ramsay-Peaty has not won a major gold medal since the 2022 Commonweath GamesByMatthew HenryBBC Sport Journalist in GlasgowIf you know what you are doing wrong, you can at least do something about it.Adam Ramsay-Peaty, however, appeared at a loss after his second bronze medal of the Commonwealth Games."Nothing makes sense this week," the 31-year-old told BBC Sport.Things that once came so easily – namely, speed and winning over one or two lengths of a swimming pool – now look out of reach.So is this the end of the road for one of Britain's greatest Olympians, or can he turn the tide in time for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028?'More training is not the answer'One thing Ramsay-Peaty, who went eight years unbeaten in the 100m from 2014 to 2022, did appear certain of was the need to change his training."I am working way too hard," he said. "I need to look at that."Former freestyler Karen Pickering, who won her last Commonwealth title aged 30 in 2002, said she thinks Ramsay-Peaty "means is he is doing too much rather than too fast".He has always been a brutally hard worker, one keen to push himself to his limits."I don't think more racing or training is the answer," Pickering said."More rest is understanding what your body needs - maybe not being around doing interviews at 11pm."It is learning to recover quicker. What do I need to eat? What do I need to drink? How do I get that lactic acid out of my body - massages or ice baths?But Scottish former breaststroker Ross Murdoch, who was Ramsay-Peaty's first rival and spent much of his career racing and training with the Englishman, said: "I know Adam and he will find it hard to take his foot off the gas."The weight of history against Ramsay-PeatyEven with a more bespoke training programme, Ramsay-Peaty cannot escape the hard facts.Only six swimmers have won Olympic gold after their 30th birthday and only two – Americans Anthony Elvin and Dana Torres in 2016 and 2000 respectively – have done so aged over 33, the age Ramsay-Peaty will be during the LA Olympics.When he returns to the pool in the European Championships next month he will face a stronger field than in Glasgow - one featuring Olympic champion Nicolo Martinenghi.Ramsay-Peaty is also facing increasing pressure from Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old from Jersey he mentors. Nowacki beat him to silver on Saturday and begins Wednesday's 200m event as favourite.Still, Pickering says there are easy gains for Ramsay-Peaty to make as he attempts to get back to the top."He has never had a good start but I would say his starts here have been pretty average," she said."He doesn't seem to be deep enough in the water."Once he would swim a 50m breaststroke, give them a head start and win because he was swimming so fast. Maybe that hasn't been a priority."I would look at those skills and go back to basics. They are a relatively simple fix."Figure caption, Peaty says 'I deserve more'Unable to deliver when it mattersWhile Ramsay-Peaty has not found his best form in Glasgow and looks unlikely to touch his best times again, it would be wrong to say he has lost his pace altogether.His time in the 100m breaststroke at the British Championships in April - 58.97 seconds - would have won Commonwealth gold. His struggles have also come amid issues away from the pool.He took a break from the sport in 2023 after issues with his mental health, and this week spoke of the "toll" external issues have taken.When he married Holly Ramsay last year his parents were not present. He has had two different coaches since his long-time mentor Mel Marshall left for a job in Australia after the 2024 Olympics."Coming into the meet, he was vocal saying his priorities have changed, that winning isn't the most important thing in his life," Murdoch said."His young family will clearly be his priority, but the expectations of how the meet was going to go certainly haven't met the reality."In his heart of hearts did he really mean the swimming isn't the priority for him?"I don't think that to be the case. I know Adam better than that. He will always want to fight and be the best he can be."'I wouldn't write him off'Ramsay-Peaty has said he wants to continue to LA.He raised the prospect of racing only the 50m event in the future, given sprint events usually suit older athletes compared to the longer distances."Adam has always had a strong 50m," Murdoch said."At the start his skills were not what set him apart from everybody. It was his raw speed and power. That is the thing that really shone through."I don't believe that has gone. It is maybe the simple things that have gone away."I don't write him off on a 100 breaststroke. That raw speed will come back as your body recovers."Pickering said: "[His pace] hasn't gone anywhere. He just couldn't access it."It is finding the best way to bring that out in an event like this."He should take some time to work through what has happened because it is a lot, but I wouldn't write him off."

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty wins bronze again - can he get back to top?

title: Detectives 'haunted' by Suzy Lamplugh case at 40 year anniversary
description: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectivesImage source, PA MediaImage caption, In this newly released imaged, Suzy Lamplugh (second left) poses w
body: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectivesImage source, PA MediaImage caption, In this newly released imaged, Suzy Lamplugh (second left) poses with her siblings, (left to right) Richard, Tamsin and LizzieUpdated 3 hours agoPolice officers investigating the disappearance of estate agent Suzy Lamplugh in west London say they remain "haunted" by the case, four decades after she went missing. Lamplugh, 25, vanished after leaving her Fulham office to meet a client on the afternoon of 28 July 1986. She never returned and her body has never been found.As the Metropolitan Police investigation is due to be mothballed next year, cold case detectives say they are troubled by the continuing mystery. To mark the 40th  anniversary of her disappearance, the Lamplugh family has  released previously unseen photographs featuring her siblings Lizzie, Tamsin and Richard and her parents Paul and Diana.In releasing the intimate family images, her siblings described her as "a truly beautiful person inside and out".Image source, HandoutImage caption, Estate agent Suzy Lamplugh went missing after meeting a client in 1986On the day she vanished, Lamplugh's diary noted an appointment with a man listed only as "Mr Kipper" in Shorrolds Road. Her white Ford Fiesta was later found abandoned nearby but there was no trace of the estate agent.She was declared "presumed dead" in 1993.Det Ch Insp Teresa Foster from the Met Police said she believed Lamplugh may have been targeted by a stalker.She had been given a desk in the office window because her employers thought she was attractive and would draw in customers.Foster said: "I'm more inclined to believe that stalking side, that someone has seen her, a predator of some type, and then lured her into a false meeting." The theory chimes with the cause taken up by Lamplugh's parents, who set up the Suzy Lamplugh Trust after she vanished. The charity campaigns on personal safety and runs the National Stalking Helpline.Foster said it was the fact Lamplugh had never been found that continued to trouble officers."It haunts myself as the senior investigating officer, and I think that comes down to the fact that Suzy's never been found," she said.Her wish, she added, is still to "bring Suzy home".Prime suspectThe investigation triggered one of the UK's biggest missing persons operations.It is also the only Met case still run on the 1980s card index system, kept in case a handwritten detail was ever overlooked.The inquiry will move to an "inactive phase" in a year's time. New information will still be followed up, but the team will no longer work the case actively.The prime suspect, John Cannan, died in prison in November 2024, while serving a sentence for the 1987 murder of Bristol newlywed Shirley Banks. A file went to prosecutors in 2002, but there was never enough to charge him and no forensic evidence has linked him to Lamplugh.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Suzy Lamplugh (third left) with her siblings, (left to right) Richard, Lizzie and Tamsin and, their parents Paul and DianaEvidence gathered from the headrest of a seat in her car using adhesive tape was sent to the US for DNA testing, but no profile could be found.  A smudged fingerprint on the rear-view mirror has also never been matched.Foster believes advances in AI or forensics could one day crack the case, or that someone may finally come forward. She pointed to two recent Met convictions that turned on relatives passing on information decades later.Janice Nix was convicted in June of the 1978 manslaughter of her five-year-old stepdaughter Andrea Bernard. In the same month, brothers Michael and Anthony Stewart were jailed for the 1984 murder of civil servant Anthony Littler.Months after Lamplugh's disappearance, her parents set up the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, which campaigns on personal safety. Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
